summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

primary_citations.citation_text: Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223 — Reporting of certain abuse or neglect of children; persons required to report (Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children, ch. 38, art. 22)
Chapter 38 — Minors; Article 22, Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children (child welfare primary)

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 30 - KANSAS DEPARTMENT FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the disposition placing a child in need of care with the noncustodial natural father, holding that the Code permitted that placement without first finding that reasonable efforts had been made to prevent removal from, or to reintegrate the child into, the home from which the child was taken.
key_cases.relevance: Reunification with a parent under the Code can mean placement with the noncustodial parent, not only return to the removal home.
key_cases.quote: the trial court was allowed to place T.S. in the custody of his natural father without first entering a finding of "reasonable efforts."

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed Kansas courts' exercise of UCCJEA jurisdiction transferred from California and held that, where minimal due process was afforded, the district court's failure to hold the statutorily required permanency hearing within 30 days did not establish a constitutional due process violation, while stressing that the statutory requirement still binds district courts.
key_cases.relevance: A late or missing permanency hearing does not by itself void the reintegration track, though the court reaffirmed that the statutory deadline is mandatory.
key_cases.quote: Mother has failed to show a constitutional due process violation resulting from the failure to comply with a Kansas statute

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that appellate courts reviewing unfitness findings view all the evidence in the light most favorable to the State, ask only whether a rational factfinder could have found unfitness highly probable, and may not reweigh evidence or reassess witness credibility.
key_cases.relevance: Where the record shows the parent rejected the services needed to make return home safe, reintegration findings will be upheld on this deferential review.
key_cases.quote: the appellate court does not weigh conflicting evidence, pass on the credibility of witnesses, or redetermine questions of fact

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights, holding that ordering a parent to undergo a clinical or substance abuse evaluation in a CINC case does not violate the Fifth Amendment, that non-compliance may be considered in the unfitness analysis, and that a parent's demonstrated unwillingness to participate in treatment may be weighed in deciding whether the State made ICWA 'active efforts.'
key_cases.relevance: Where reunification fails, the adequacy of the agency's reunification efforts is measured against the parent's own willingness to engage.
key_cases.quote: we do not find Mother's reluctance to participate in individual therapy meant SFM did not engage in active efforts to persuade her to do so

key_cases.case_name: Bolyard ex rel. Bolyard v. Kansas Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for SRS and its caseworker, holding that placing children who were in SRS temporary custody with their mother, and the means chosen to monitor that placement, were discretionary functions immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act because no clearly defined mandatory duty or guideline required a different course.
key_cases.relevance: Placing a child in agency custody back with a parent is the archetypal discretionary judgment, and the adequacy of the agency's supervision of that placement is not reviewable in tort.
key_cases.quote: The discretionary function exception is applicable only when no clearly defined mandatory duty or guideline exists which the government agency is required to follow
